4EC1|P58384A|P2|Q1(g).stimulus_text: In November 2018, Mexico’s current account deficit increased to $5.082bn.
4EC1|P58384A|P2|Q1(g).subtopic: Current account: causes of a deficit; trade in goods and services
4EC1|P58384A|P2|Q1(g).reasoning_skill_family: Domestic quality and competitiveness -> imports or exports -> current account balance
4EC1|P58384A|P2|Q1(g).source_evidence: QP PDF page 5: Mexico current-account stimulus and 1(g) stem; QP cover is 4EC1/02, log P58384A. MS cover identifies January 2020, Paper 02. MS PDF page 6, key 1(g), gives AO2 3-mark alternatives: poor domestic quality shifts purchases toward imports, or reduces exports; either contributes to the $5.082bn deficit. The following Australia/India/WTO subsidy passage is not part of this item.
4EC1|P58384A|P2|Q1(g).reviewer_note: Checked against the page-level QP/MS text and source covers; page image review is still pending. Do not infer other Mexico facts beyond the supplied deficit and quality premise. Mark-scheme routes are alternatives, not cumulative requirements.

4EC1|P62031A|P2|Q3(d).stimulus_text: In 2018, Italy entered a recession after the country’s manufacturing sector decreased for the third month in a row. Gross domestic product (GDP) fell by 0.1% from July to September.
4EC1|P62031A|P2|Q3(d).subtopic: Unemployment: cyclical unemployment and the economic cycle
4EC1|P62031A|P2|Q3(d).reasoning_skill_family: Recession / falling aggregate demand -> lower output and derived labour demand -> cyclical unemployment
4EC1|P62031A|P2|Q3(d).source_evidence: QP PDF page 15: Italy manufacturing contracted for a third month, GDP fell 0.1% July–September, followed by 3(d). QP log P62031A and 4EC1/02 cover print Friday 5 June 2020. The paired MS cover identifies November 2020, Paper 2. MS PDF page 13, key 3(d), discusses recession, lower consumption/investment and confidence, lower orders, firms requiring fewer workers/cutting recruitment, and rising unemployment. The following China interest-rate stimulus belongs to 3(e), not 3(d). QP/MS item content aligns, but the sitting-label conflict remains unresolved.
4EC1|P62031A|P2|Q3(d).reviewer_note: Keep the question indexed under the QP's May-June 2020 source label pending a verified identity decision. Preserve MS cover session November 2020 as a conflict; do not silently rewrite either source. Page image review remains pending. MS content is indicative, not a checklist.

4EC1|P60749A|P1|Q1(h).prompt_text: Explain one reason why the demand for these tickets might be price inelastic.
4EC1|P60749A|P1|Q1(h).stimulus_text: Concert tickets to see the most popular music artists can sell for very high prices.
4EC1|P60749A|P1|Q1(h).subtopic: Price elasticity of demand; determinants including availability of substitutes
4EC1|P60749A|P1|Q1(h).reasoning_skill_family: PED—few/no close substitutes for the specific experience -> limited switching after a price rise -> relatively small change in quantity demanded
4EC1|P60749A|P1|Q1(h).source_evidence: QP PDF p.4: exact 1(h) question and concert-ticket context. MS PDF p.6, 1(h): AO2 3 marks, one relevant reason, development, and music-concert context; accepted content includes no substitutes for seeing the artist live, leading the consumer to pay a high amount. This is paraphrased in teaching; the quoted question stem is checked.
4EC1|P60749A|P1|Q1(h).reviewer_note: The QP supplies that these are tickets for popular artists and may sell for high prices; lack of close substitutes is the mark-scheme reason, not a separately supplied fact about every concert. Explain conditionally rather than inventing sold-out status or buyer behaviour.

4EC1|P73498A|P1|Q4(b).prompt_text: With reference to the data above and your knowledge of economics, analyse why price elasticity of demand (PED) may be relatively inelastic at Marina Café.
4EC1|P73498A|P1|Q4(b).stimulus_text: Marina Café is popular with tourists and locals in the town of Budva, Montenegro. It is situated next to the sea, with views of the surrounding mountains. Customers can enjoy their drinks whilst benefitting from the pleasant surroundings but pay €2.00 for a cup of coffee. The same brand of coffee can be bought for €0.80 a cup in some other cafés in Budva.
4EC1|P73498A|P1|Q4(b).subtopic: Price elasticity of demand; close substitutes, product differentiation and share of income
4EC1|P73498A|P1|Q4(b).reasoning_skill_family: PED—substitution and differentiated experience: location/experience makes other products less close substitutes -> weaker switching after a price rise -> relatively small fall in quantity demanded
4EC1|P73498A|P1|Q4(b).er_guidance_reference: Q4(b): use the café location/scenery to explain why the cheaper café may not be a close substitute; do not merely repeat prices/context.
4EC1|P73498A|P1|Q4(b).source_evidence: QP PDF p.19 contains the Marina Café context and Q4(b) stem. MS PDF p.19 has the same task and AO2 (3)/AO3 (3) indicative content: location/scenery can make the experience distinctive, reducing close substitutes; it also notes coffee is a small share of income. The November 2023 P1 examiner-report digest maps Q4(b) to this case and cautions against merely repeating the data.
4EC1|P73498A|P1|Q4(b).reviewer_note: The café context is given; whether the alternatives are close substitutes is a reasoned inference. Do not assume every customer values the scenery. If a customer only wants the same coffee, the cheaper café may be a closer substitute. The question says “may be”; this is a conditional, not universal, effect.

4EC1|P75954A|P1|Q1(h).prompt_text: Explain one reason why demand for a product, such as a soft drink, usually becomes more price elastic over time.
4EC1|P75954A|P1|Q1(h).stimulus_text: Six months after the price for a soft drink increased, its price elasticity of demand (PED) changed from –1.5 to –2.0.
4EC1|P75954A|P1|Q1(h).subtopic: Price elasticity of demand; time and consumer adjustment/substitutes
4EC1|P75954A|P1|Q1(h).reasoning_skill_family: PED—time to adjust: habits/limited alternatives initially constrain switching -> more time permits behaviour change or entry/substitutes -> quantity demanded responds more to price
4EC1|P75954A|P1|Q1(h).er_guidance_status: REMOTE_REPORT_IDENTITY_MATCHED_AND_SUMMARIZED; item-level locator in digest; PDF not local
4EC1|P75954A|P1|Q1(h).er_guidance_reference: Q1(h): one reason, context and a developed cause/consequence; “more elastic over time” needs the time mechanism, not just a label.
4EC1|P75954A|P1|Q1(h).source_evidence: QP PDF p.5 gives the soft-drink PED change from −1.5 to −2.0 and Q1(h). MS PDF p.6, key 1(h), awards 1 mark each for a relevant reason, development and context; it accepts habit adjustment over time or increased market entry/substitutes. The November 2024 P1 ER digest has an identity-matched Q1(h) note. The report PDF is remote-only in the repository; no script or quotation is reproduced.
4EC1|P75954A|P1|Q1(h).reviewer_note: The supplied figures show PED becoming more elastic in absolute value by 0.5 after six months. The “habit breaks” and “more firms enter” explanations are alternative routes; do not combine as mandatory steps. Limits include persistent habit or few substitutes. Do not claim every soft-drink buyer will change.
